t: Is Your Free Zone Company a Qualifying Free Zone Person? The Conditions, Activities and Traps
d: The six conditions to be a Qualifying Free Zone Person and get 0% UAE Corporate Tax, the qualifying and excluded activities under Ministerial Decision 229 of 2025, the de minimis test, and the five-year cost of failing.
c: “We’re in a free zone, so we pay 0%.” It’s the most common Corporate Tax assumption I see, and it’s wrong more often than people expect. The 0% rate belongs to a Qualifying Free Zone Person (QFZP) , not to the licence or the zone. A company has to earn it by meeting every condition, in every tax period. And the 0% only applies to Qualifying Income . Anything else it earns is taxed at 9%. First: it’s the company that qualifies, not the zone People search for “is my free zone a qualifying free zone”. There’s no such category. Two separate things have to be true: The zone must be a Free Zone for Corporate Tax purposes. Your free zone authority can confirm it. (The four zone tests ) The company must meet the QFZP conditions below. The six conditions Adequate substance in the free zone. Its core income-generating activities happen in the free zone, with enough qualified full-time staff, assets and operating spending for the business. A registered address with no people doesn’t pass. It earns Qualifying Income. Broadly, income from transactions with other Free Zone Persons, and from qualifying activities with anyone else, as long as the activity isn’t an excluded one. Non-qualifying revenue stays within de minimis. It must not exceed 5% of total revenue or AED 5 million, whichever is lower . It hasn’t elected the standard rates. Opting into the normal 9% regime gives up QFZP status. It follows transfer pricing rules. Related-party transactions at arm’s length, with a Master File and Local File where the thresholds require them. It prepares audited financial statements. Ministerial Decision No. 229 of 2025 requires them for every QFZP, in line with Ministerial Decision No. 84 of 2025 , regardless of revenue. Which activities qualify, and which never do Ministerial Decision No. 229 of 2025 replaced the 2023 list in September 2025, with effect from 1 June 2023. Qualifying activities: manufacturing of goods or materials, and processing of goods or materials trading of qualifying commodities holding shares and other securities for investment ownership, management and operation of ships reinsurance, fund management, and wealth and investment management services headquarter services to related parties treasury and financing services to related parties, or for its own account financing and leasing of aircraft distribution of goods or materials in or from a Designated Zone logistics services activities ancillary to any of the above Excluded activities: dealings with individuals, except certain ship, fund management, wealth management and aircraft activities banking insurance, except where it falls within reinsurance or headquarter services finance and leasing, except the qualifying ones above owning or operating immovable property, except commercial property in a free zone transacted with Free Zone Persons activities ancillary to these The traps that cost the 0% Selling to individuals. A free zone trader whose customers include walk-in or online retail buyers is dealing with individuals. That revenue is non-qualifying, and it counts against the de minimis limit. Distribution outside a Designated Zone. Distribution only qualifies if it runs in or from a zone that is a Designated Zone for Corporate Tax, the goods are imported through that zone, and the buyer resells or processes them. (Distribution conditions ) Commodity trading by a logistics-heavy business. Trading of qualifying commodities doesn’t qualify if 51% or more of the company’s revenue in the tax period comes from distribution, warehousing, logistics or inventory management. Breaching de minimis by a small amount. On AED 40 million of revenue, the limit is AED 2 million (5%). On AED 200 million, it’s AED 5 million (the cap). One unusual contract can tip a company over. Skipping the audit. No audited financial statements, no QFZP status, however clean the activities are. The cost of failing: five years, not one If a QFZP fails any condition at any point in a tax period, it stops bei Is every company in a UAE free zone taxed at 0%? No. Only a Qualifying Free Zone Person that meets every condition gets 0%, and only on its Qualifying Income. Other taxable income is taxed at 9%, and a free zone company that doesn't qualify is taxed at the standard rates. What is the de minimis rule for Qualifying Free Zone Persons? Non-qualifying revenue in a tax period must not exceed 5% of total revenue or AED 5 million, whichever is lower. Breaching it costs QFZP status for that period and the next four. Can a Qualifying Free Zone Person sell to individuals? Dealings with individuals are an excluded activity under Ministerial Decision No. 229 of 2025, with narrow exceptions for certain ship, fund management, wealth management and aircraft activities. Income from them counts as non-qualifying revenue. Does a Qualifying Free Zone Person need audited financial statements? Yes. Ministerial Decision No. 229 of 2025 requires every Qualifying Free Zone Person to prepare audited financial statements in accordance with Ministerial Decision No. 84 of 2025, whatever its revenue. Is my free zone a qualifying free zone? The test is on the company, not the zone. The zone must be a Free Zone for Corporate Tax purposes, which your free zone authority can confirm, and the company must then meet the QFZP conditions itself.

t: Vending Machines and UAE VAT: No Tax Invoice Needed, but the Records and Dates Still Matter
d: FTA Directive on Tax Transactions No. 8 of 2026 explained: no tax invoice for vending machine sales, the minimum records to keep, what counts as a vending machine, and when VAT is due if a third party runs the machine.
c: On 19 November 2026 the FTA issued Directive on Tax Transactions No. 8 of 2026 , on the VAT treatment of vending machines. It’s short, three pages, and it settles two practical questions: whether every vending sale needs a tax invoice, and when VAT is due when someone else runs the machine. 1. No tax invoice for vending machine sales A Taxable Person supplying goods or services through a vending machine doesn’t have to issue a tax invoice for those supplies. The condition: it must keep sufficient records to substantiate the details of the supplies . So the obligation moves from the invoice to the records. The VAT is still due. What goes away is the paperwork per sale. 2. The minimum records The directive sets the minimum. Your records must show: a description of the goods or services supplied, the total consideration received and the VAT charged , and the date of supply , as set by Article 26(2) of the VAT Law . If your machines report sales electronically, that report is likely to be the core of these records. If they don’t, you need another reliable way to capture what was sold and when the money was collected. 3. What counts as a vending machine The directive defines a vending machine as an automated self-service device used to supply goods or services automatically and immediately , as a result of direct physical interaction by the customer , without any human intervention by the supplier . Running, maintaining, monitoring or restocking the machine doesn’t count as human intervention. So a machine that staff refill each morning still qualifies. A sale where a staff member takes the order or hands over the goods doesn’t. 4. When someone else runs the machine Many businesses place machines with an operator who collects the money and reports back. For that case, the directive fixes the date the consideration is treated as collected through the machine, for Article 26(2). It’s the earlier of: the date the Taxable Person receives information from the operator confirming the collection and the amount collected , or the day after 30 days from the operator’s collection. The 30-day backstop matters. A slow monthly report from the operator doesn’t delay your VAT. If the operator collected on 2 March and only reports in April, the consideration is treated as collected on the day after 30 days from 2 March, and the sale belongs in the VAT return for that period. What to do now Check each machine against the definition. Automated, immediate, no staff involved in the sale. Make sure your sales reports capture all three minimum fields (description, total and VAT, date of supply) for every machine. If a third party operates your machines, review the contract. Ask for collection reports well inside 30 days, showing the date and amount of each collection. Reconcile operator reports to bank receipts each VAT period, and keep both. Map the dates to your VAT periods using the earlier-of rule, so sales near the period end land in the right return. Source: FTA Directive on Tax Transactions No. 8 of 2026 for Value Added Tax on the Tax Treatment of Vending Machines, issued 19 November 2026, to be published in the Official Gazette. Do vending machine sales need a tax invoice in the UAE? No. Under FTA Directive No. 8 of 2026, a Taxable Person selling goods or services through a vending machine doesn't have to issue a tax invoice, provided it keeps sufficient records of the supplies. What records are needed for vending machine sales? At a minimum: a description of the goods or services supplied, the total consideration received and VAT charged, and the date of supply under Article 26(2) of the VAT Law. What counts as a vending machine for UAE VAT? An automated self-service device that supplies goods or services automatically and immediately when the customer physically interacts with it, with no human intervention by the supplier. Running, maintaining, monitoring or restocking the machine doesn't count as human intervention. When is VAT due if someone else operates my vending machine? The consideration is treated as collected on the earlier of the date the operator confirms the collection and the amount, or the day after 30 days from the date the operator collected it.

t: E-Invoicing Goes Live on 1 January: A Six-Week Readiness Plan for AED 50m+ Businesses
d: A week-by-week plan for UAE businesses with AED 50 million+ revenue to be ready for mandatory e-invoicing on 1 January 2027: scope, data, testing, controls and cut-over.
c: If your business had revenue of AED 50 million or more in its latest financial statements, e-invoicing becomes mandatory on 1 January 2027 . That’s six weeks from now, with National Day and the year-end close in between. This is a week-by-week plan to get there. Every rule in it comes from the Ministry of Finance’s E-Invoicing Guidelines v2.0 , Ministerial Decision No. 197 of 2026 and Cabinet Decision No. 173 of 2026 . Each one has a full guide on this site, linked below. Week of 23 November: scope and ASP Confirm the phase for each entity , on revenue in its latest financial statements. The guidelines don’t say whether revenue is added up across a group, so test each entity on its own figures. (Who must comply ) List what’s excluded: sales to consumers, imports, exempt and zero-rated financial services, and transactions inside the same VAT Tax Group until 31 December 2028. A Corporate Tax Group doesn’t count. (MD 197 explained ) Check the ASP is signed and that onboarding has started from the e-invoicing tile in EmaraTax . The deadline to appoint was 30 October 2026 . If you haven’t, this is the only job this week. (Choosing an ASP ) Get a TIN for any in-scope entity without a TRN, and note each entity’s Peppol ID : 0235 followed by its 10-digit TIN. Week of 30 November: data Map your invoices against the mandatory fields. There are 51 under PINT-AE, plus conditional ones. The usual gaps are buyer legal registration details and electronic addresses. (The five-corner model ) Clean the customer master: collect each customer’s TRN (or TIN if not VAT-registered). Never put a Corporate Tax TRN in the VAT number field. Tag intra-VAT-group invoices in the ERP so they can be excluded now and brought in on 1 January 2029. Week of 7 December: testing Test end to end with your ASP: sending, receiving and FTA reporting, with real scenarios. Include the awkward invoices: a credit note covering several invoices, an advance and its final invoice, a foreign-currency invoice and a zero-rated sale. Send one that fails on purpose , so you see how a rejection comes back and who receives it. Week of 14 December: controls The 14-business-day rule. E-invoices and credit notes must be issued and transmitted within 14 business days of the transaction. VAT timing rules still apply alongside it, so build both into the billing cut-off. Rejections. Name who monitors failed invoices and how quickly they’re fixed. The 14-day clock doesn’t stop while an invoice sits in an error queue. Customers who aren’t live yet. You still issue the e-invoice through your ASP, to the placeholder endpoint 0235:9900000098 , and also send a normal tax invoice, such as a PDF, so they can recover input VAT. Week of 21 December: receiving and archive Get accounts payable ready to receive. The penalty for failing to implement applies to recipients too, not only to issuers. (Penalties ) Agree archive terms. You must keep e-invoice data for the Tax Procedures Law period, generally 5 years. If the ASP or ERP host stores it, make sure the contract gives you access and export for that whole period. Set a data-change routine. Not telling your ASP about changes to your FTA-registered details costs AED 250 a day. Add it to the licence-renewal checklist. 28 December to 1 January: go live Sign off the cut-over plan: which invoices go out the old way before 1 January, and which go through the ASP from then on. Check the first invoices daily in the first week: delivered, accepted, reported. Start an outage log. There’s no longer a duty to report system failures, but an outage doesn’t stop the 14-day clock. If you’re not going to make it Say so early, and keep going. The penalty for failing to implement is AED 5,000 for the first instance, then AED 5,000 for each month or part of a month it continues, capped at AED 50,000 in any 12 months . Every month you’re live sooner saves money. The per-invoice penalty, AED 100 an invoice capped at AED 5,000 a month, matters less than the commercial cos When does UAE e-invoicing start for large businesses? Businesses with revenue of AED 50 million or more in their latest financial statements must go live by 1 January 2027. The deadline to appoint an ASP was 30 October 2026. What happens if my business isn't live on 1 January 2027? Not implementing e-invoicing, including not appointing an ASP, is penalised at AED 5,000 for the first instance and AED 5,000 for each month it continues, capped at AED 50,000 in any 12 months. Can I still send PDF invoices after go-live? The legal invoice is the e-invoice sent through your ASP. A PDF can go alongside it, and to customers who aren't live yet you must also send a normal tax invoice so they can recover input VAT. How long do I have to issue an e-invoice? E-invoices and e-credit notes must be issued and transmitted within 14 business days of the transaction, subject to the VAT Law's own timing rules.

t: Family Foundations and UAE Corporate Tax: Taxed, or Transparent?
d: How UAE Corporate Tax treats a family foundation: when it is taxed at 9%, the five conditions to be treated as transparent, registration, returns and what beneficiaries must do.
c: Families are increasingly holding wealth, property and investments through foundations and trusts in the UAE. Corporate Tax gives these structures a choice: be taxed like a company, or be treated as transparent so the foundation itself pays nothing. The FTA’s Basic Tax Information Bulletin on the Treatment of a Family Foundation (October 2026) sets out how that choice works. Here is what it means in practice. What counts as a family foundation For Corporate Tax, a Family Foundation is any foundation, trust or similar entity set up to hold and manage family wealth for its beneficiaries, and that meets the conditions below. One exception matters: a company such as an LLC is not “similar to a foundation or trust” , so it can’t be a Family Foundation, unless it is wholly owned and controlled by one. Route 1: taxed like a company (the default) A family foundation that is a juridical person is, by default, a Taxable Person in its own right. It: registers on EmaraTax as a Taxable Person, pays Corporate Tax at 0% on Taxable Income up to AED 375,000 and 9% above , or, if it is a Qualifying Free Zone Person, 0% on Qualifying Income and 9% on the rest, and files a Tax Return within 9 months of the end of each Tax Period. Route 2: transparent, with FTA approval A transparent foundation isn’t taxed itself. It’s treated as an Unincorporated Partnership , and its members are taxed on their share of its assets, liabilities, income and expenses. A foundation that is not a juridical person is transparent already, and registers on EmaraTax as an Unincorporated Partnership. A foundation that is a juridical person has to qualify and apply. The five conditions to be transparent Under Ministerial Decision No. 261 of 2024 and FTA Decision No. 5 of 2025 , a family foundation that is a juridical person is treated as transparent only if all five are met: Beneficiaries: it was set up for identified or identifiable individuals, a public benefit entity, or both. Activity: its main activity is receiving, holding, investing, disbursing or disposing of savings and investment assets, or otherwise managing them. No business: it does nothing that would be a Business if the founder, settlor or a beneficiary did it directly or held the assets themselves. Purpose: avoiding Corporate Tax is not its main or principal purpose. Approval: it applies to the FTA to be treated as an Unincorporated Partnership, and the FTA approves. Miss any one, or don’t get approval, and the foundation stays taxable. The timing matters. The application must be made before the end of the Tax Period it applies to. It can take effect from the current Tax Period, the next one, or another date the FTA sets. Condition 3 is the one to test hardest. The question isn’t what the foundation calls itself, but whether the same activity, done by the founder or a beneficiary personally, would count as a Business for Corporate Tax. A foundation running a trading operation, for example, would fail it. Registration and filing, side by side   Taxed (opaque) Transparent Register on EmaraTax Yes, as a Taxable Person Yes, as an Unincorporated Partnership (or registered, then approved) Tax Return Within 9 months of year end Not required Annual confirmation Not applicable Within 9 months of year end Who pays tax The foundation Beneficiaries that are Taxable Persons, on their share Every family foundation formed under UAE law has to register , one way or the other. A juridical-person foundation registers as a Taxable Person first, and can then apply for transparency. What beneficiaries need to do Individual beneficiaries only register and file if they run a business in the UAE outside the foundation and its turnover is over AED 1 million in a calendar year. Beneficiaries that are Taxable Persons , such as a public benefit entity, register in their own right and include their share of a transparent foundation’s results in their own Tax Return. Penalties Missing a registration, return or annual confirmation can att Do UAE family foundations pay Corporate Tax? A family foundation that is a juridical person pays Corporate Tax at 0% up to AED 375,000 of Taxable Income and 9% above, unless the FTA approves it as a fiscally transparent Unincorporated Partnership. Can a family foundation be tax transparent in the UAE? Yes, if it benefits identified individuals or a public benefit entity, mainly holds and invests assets, conducts no business, isn't mainly for tax avoidance, and the FTA approves its application before the end of the Tax Period. Does a transparent family foundation still register and file? It still registers on EmaraTax. It doesn't file a Tax Return, but it must file an annual confirmation within 9 months of the end of each Tax Period. Do beneficiaries of a family foundation need to register for Corporate Tax? Individual beneficiaries only need to register if their own UAE business turnover is over AED 1 million in a calendar year. Beneficiaries that are Taxable Persons, such as a public benefit entity, register and report their share.

t: Free Zone or Designated Zone? Your Address Has to Pass Four Different Tax Tests
d: FTA Public Clarification TAXP010 explained: the four Free Zone and Designated Zone tests for Corporate Tax, VAT and Excise Tax, and why distributors can lose the 0% rate.
c: “We’re in a free zone, so we’re fine.” I hear it often. For tax, it doesn’t settle much. On 2 October 2026 the FTA published Public Clarification TAXP010, Free Zones and Designated Zones for Tax Purposes . Its point is simple: Corporate Tax, VAT and Excise Tax each define these zones differently, and you must check your location against each law separately. Four tests, not one TAXP010 names four categories: Corporate Tax Free Zone Corporate Tax Designated Zone Excise Tax Designated Zone VAT Designated Zone One business can be in a Corporate Tax Free Zone without being in a VAT Designated Zone. Or in a VAT Designated Zone without the location counting as a Designated Zone for Corporate Tax. 1. Corporate Tax Free Zone A Free Zone for Corporate Tax is a defined geographic area in the UAE named in a Cabinet Decision , issued on the Minister’s suggestion. This is the starting point for the 0% regime. A Qualifying Free Zone Person must be incorporated, established or registered in a Free Zone, and operate from it, to get 0% on its Qualifying Income. 2. Corporate Tax Designated Zone This is the one the clarification is really about. A Designated Zone for Corporate Tax is a zone that is a Designated Zone under the VAT Law and included as a Free Zone under the Corporate Tax Law. A VAT Designated Zone is not automatically a Designated Zone for Corporate Tax. It must pass both tests. TAXP010 tells taxpayers to confirm with their free zone authority whether they are in a Free Zone or a Designated Zone for Corporate Tax. 3. Excise Tax Designated Zone For Excise Tax, a Designated Zone is either: a fenced free zone that has security measures restricting the movement of people and excise goods in and out, is controlled and supervised by a customs department, and has an appointed Warehouse Keeper ; or any other area the FTA specifies , provided it is a specific geographic area with the same kind of security measures and an appointed Warehouse Keeper. The Warehouse Keeper has to apply to the FTA to register the area. To confirm, ask your free zone authority , or the Warehouse Keeper whether the FTA has approved the area. 4. VAT Designated Zone A VAT Designated Zone is a fenced area listed in Cabinet Decision No. 59 of 2017 (as amended). Being on that list is not the whole test: under Article 51(1) of the VAT Executive Regulation , it is only treated as outside the UAE for VAT if: it is a specific fenced area with security measures and customs controls over people and goods moving in and out, it has internal procedures for keeping, storing and processing goods, and its operator complies with the FTA’s procedures. So TAXP010 asks for two checks : find your zone on the FTA’s published list, then confirm with the free zone authority that the specific area where you’re based meets Article 51(1). Why distributors should care most Under Ministerial Decision No. 229 of 2025 , one of the Qualifying Activities for a Qualifying Free Zone Person is distribution of goods or materials in or from a Designated Zone . Being in a free zone isn’t enough for this activity. The distribution itself has to run in or from a Corporate Tax Designated Zone , and it has to meet every condition: What counts: buying and selling goods, materials, component parts or other tangible or movable items. It can include importing, storage, inventory management, handling, transport and export. Where: in or from a Designated Zone, with goods entering the UAE imported through that zone. Who buys: a customer who resells, processes or alters the goods for sale or resale, or a public benefit entity. Procedures: any additional procedures the FTA prescribes, on top of every other Qualifying Free Zone Person condition. The cost of getting it wrong is high. If a Qualifying Free Zone Person fails any condition at any point in a tax period, it stops being a Qualifying Free Zone Person from the start of that period and for the next four . That’s five tax periods at the standard rates. What to do Is every UAE free zone a Designated Zone? No. A free zone is only a VAT Designated Zone if it is listed in Cabinet Decision No. 59 of 2017 and meets the conditions in Article 51(1) of the VAT Executive Regulation. Corporate Tax and Excise Tax have their own separate tests. Is a VAT Designated Zone automatically a Designated Zone for Corporate Tax? No. TAXP010 says the zone must be both a VAT Designated Zone and a Free Zone for Corporate Tax purposes. Confirm it with your free zone authority. Can a Qualifying Free Zone Person get 0% on distribution income? Only if the distribution is carried out in or from a Corporate Tax Designated Zone, goods entering the UAE are imported through that zone, the buyer resells, processes or alters the goods for sale or is a public benefit entity, and every other QFZP condition is met. What happens if a Qualifying Free Zone Person fails a condition? It stops being a Qualifying Free Zone Person from the start of that tax period and for the next four tax periods.

t: The Bank Compared Our Client's VAT Returns With Its Bank Credits. They Didn't Match.
d: A real case: a bank found VAT returns didn't match bank credits at facility renewal. How we reconciled it, why it led to a voluntary disclosure, and how to check first.
c: Banks used to look at your audited accounts. Many now also look at your VAT returns, and compare them with the money going into your account. This is a case from my practice, with the client’s details left out. What happened A client applied to renew a bank facility. As part of its review, the bank compared the sales in the client’s VAT returns with the credits in its bank statements . The two didn’t match, and the bank asked for an explanation before it would go ahead. How we resolved it We reconciled the bank credits to the sales in the returns. Most of the gap had ordinary explanations: money coming in that wasn’t sales, and timing. After those, a balance was left that was sales which hadn’t been reported in the VAT returns . The client filed a voluntary disclosure to correct the returns, and the reconciliation went back to the bank with the explanation. What the reconciliation looks like With illustrative figures:   AED Total credits in the bank statements 9,400,000 Less: loans drawn and capital introduced (1,100,000) Less: transfers between the company’s own accounts (650,000) Less: refunds and other non-sales receipts (150,000) Adjust: timing of customer receipts (100,000) Sales receipts that should be in the returns 7,400,000 Sales in the VAT returns, including VAT 7,140,000 Unexplained 260,000 Compare like with like. Bank receipts include VAT, so compare them with sales including VAT. And include zero-rated and exempt sales, which are reported in their own boxes of the return. The usual reconciling items Loans and capital: facility drawdowns, shareholder loans and capital injections. Own-account transfers: money moved between the company’s own bank accounts appears as a credit in one of them. Refunds and other receipts: supplier refunds, returned deposits, insurance claims and VAT refunds. Timing: cash received this year for last year’s sales, and this year’s sales still unpaid at year end. Zero-rated and exempt sales: these belong in their own boxes of the return. Check they were reported there and not left out. Sales left out of the returns: whatever remains after all of the above. That needs correcting. Keep a document for every line. “Loan from shareholder” with nothing behind it won’t satisfy a bank, an auditor or the FTA. When the gap is unreported sales Unreported sales mean the VAT returns were wrong, so this stops being only a bank matter. The Tax Procedures rules decide how to correct it: Over AED 10,000 of tax: file a voluntary disclosure within 20 business days of becoming aware of the error. AED 10,000 or less: you can correct it in the return for the period in which you found it. A voluntary disclosure carries penalties, but they’re lower than if the FTA finds the error in an audit. The Penalty Estimator compares the two for your figures. Run the check before anyone asks Reconcile bank credits to sales every quarter, before you file the VAT return. As a routine it takes an afternoon. In the middle of a facility renewal, it takes weeks. Tag non-sales receipts as they come in: loans, capital, transfers and refunds. Year-end reconciliation becomes a report instead of a project. Keep a short note and a document for every reconciling item. Fix errors promptly, through the next return or a voluntary disclosure, depending on the amount. Your auditor runs the same test at year end: see what your auditor actually tests in your VAT returns . The other case in this pair: the FTA query that followed a customer’s tax evasion . Facing the same question from your bank? Ask me about it . Why would my bank compare VAT returns with bank credits? To check that the sales in your VAT returns are consistent with the money coming into your account before it renews or extends a facility. What explains a gap between bank credits and VAT sales? Loans and capital, transfers between your own accounts, refunds and other non-sales receipts, timing, and zero-rated or exempt sales. Whatever is left may be unreported sales. How do I correct unreported sales found in the reconciliation? Over AED 10,000 of tax: file a voluntary disclosure within 20 business days of becoming aware. AED 10,000 or less: correct it in the return for the period you found it.

t: The FTA Asked About Our Client's Sales Because a Customer Evaded Tax
d: A real case: a customer was found guilty of tax evasion and the FTA asked our client for the detail behind its VAT returns. Why documents ended it, and what to keep.
c: You can file every VAT return correctly and still get a letter from the FTA, because of something one of your customers did. This is a case from my practice, with the client’s details left out. What happened A client received an email from the FTA asking for a detailed breakdown behind VAT returns it had already submitted. Our client hadn’t done anything wrong. The reason for the request was that one of the client’s customers had been found guilty of tax evasion , and the FTA was looking at the transactions connected to that customer. When the FTA investigates one business, it looks at who that business bought from and sold to. Every supplier and customer in that chain can be asked to show their side of the transactions. How it ended The client had the documents. Every sale to that customer was backed by the invoice and its supporting records, and the sales tied to what was reported in the returns. The client faced no legal complications. The FTA asked for documents, the documents answered the question, and the matter ended there. What the client took from it Their VAT had been right all along. What protected them was being able to show it was right: quickly, completely, and with paper behind every number. Without those records, the same email could have become a much longer review of their returns, at a time when the FTA was already looking closely at that customer. You don’t control who your customers are or what they do. You control whether your side of every transaction is documented. What to have ready for every sale For each customer Trade licence and TRN, checked on the FTA’s TRN verification tool The contract, quotation or purchase order Who you deal with there, and their authority to act For each sale The tax invoice, and any credit notes A delivery note or other proof the goods or services were provided The payment received into your account, matched to the invoice For each VAT return A sales listing that adds up to the sales reported in the return A reconciliation of the return to the ledger Workings for any adjustments Keep these for the full record-keeping period, generally five years. If you receive a request like this Read the request carefully. Note exactly which periods, customers and documents it asks for, and the deadline it gives. Pull the sales file for every transaction in scope: invoices, orders, delivery proof and payments. Tie it to the returns. Show that the sales listing adds up to what you reported for each period. Explain any differences with a document for each: credit notes, timing, or errors. If you find a real error, correct it. Errors over AED 10,000 of tax need a voluntary disclosure; the Penalty Estimator shows what that costs. Reply complete and on time, as one organised pack, and keep a copy of exactly what you sent. If the request is unclear or covers a large volume, get help early rather than close to the deadline. The purchase side is now stricter too This case was about sales. On purchases, the bar has risen: since 1 October 2026, FTA Decision No. 13 lets the FTA reject your input VAT if a supplier in your chain evaded tax and you should have been aware of it. The five-part Decision No. 13 series covers the checks, and the Supplier Verification tool builds the record for each supplier. The other case in this pair: a bank that compared VAT returns with bank credits . Had a similar request? Ask me about it . Why would the FTA ask about my VAT returns if I did nothing wrong? If one of your customers or suppliers is investigated for evasion, the FTA can ask every business in that chain for its side of the transactions. What should I keep for each sale? The tax invoice and credit notes, delivery proof, the matched payment, the customer's licence and verified TRN, and a sales listing that ties to each return. What if I find an error while answering an FTA request? Correct it. Errors over AED 10,000 of tax need a voluntary disclosure.

t: The New UAE E-Invoicing Penalties: Cabinet Decision No. 173 of 2026 Explained
d: The four UAE e-invoicing penalties under Cabinet Decision No. 173 of 2026, the new AED 50,000 cap, what changed from Decision 106 of 2025, with worked examples.
c: On 30 October 2026, the Ministry of Finance announced Cabinet Decision No. 173 of 2026 , a new penalty table for e-invoicing. It repeals Cabinet Decision No. 106 of 2025 , so the figures still quoted in many articles are out of date. Overall it’s softer. But one penalty now also applies to recipients, and the largest one still starts the day you miss your date. The four penalties Violation Penalty Cap Not implementing e-invoicing under Ministerial Decision No. 244, including not appointing an ASP ; or a recipient that has implemented but doesn’t keep up its recipient obligations AED 5,000 for the first instance, then AED 5,000 for each month or part of a month it continues AED 50,000 in any 12 consecutive months Not issuing and transmitting an e-invoice to the recipient through the system AED 100 per e-invoice AED 5,000 per calendar month Not issuing and transmitting an e-credit note AED 100 per credit note AED 5,000 per calendar month Not telling your ASP about changes to your data registered with the FTA AED 250 per day or part of a day AED 5,000 per calendar month The decision takes effect the day after it’s published in the Official Gazette. What changed from Decision No. 106 of 2025 The implementation penalty is now capped at AED 50,000 in any 12 months. Under the old table it ran at AED 5,000 a month with no overall cap. Recipients are now covered. The implementation penalty applies to an issuer or a recipient that fails to implement. It also catches a recipient that went live but stopped meeting its obligations. The data-change penalty is lower. It drops from AED 1,000 a day to AED 250 a day , with a monthly cap of AED 5,000. The system-failure penalty is gone. The AED 1,000-a-day penalty for not reporting a system failure has been removed, in line with Ministerial Decision No. 197 , which repealed the duty to report. No double penalties. If the same person is both issuer and recipient for the same violation, only one penalty applies. What hasn’t changed: voluntary e-invoicing is never penalised. If you go live before your mandatory date, mistakes made before that date don’t attract these penalties. What it costs in practice A Phase 1 business that isn’t live on 1 January 2027. AED 5,000 for the first instance, then AED 5,000 for each month or part of a month it stays non-compliant. On those figures it reaches the AED 50,000 cap after about nine more months. The cap applies to any 12-month period, so it isn’t a one-off. Invoices emailed as PDFs instead of going through the ASP. 120 invoices in March at AED 100 each is AED 12,000. That’s capped at AED 5,000 for March , and the cap resets each calendar month. A trade licence change not passed to the ASP. Told 12 days late: 12 × AED 250 = AED 3,000 . These sit on top of ordinary VAT penalties. If an invoice wasn’t issued properly, the VAT questions (output tax timing, your customer’s input tax claim) still apply under the VAT rules. For those, see the penalty calculator . Where the risk really is The per-invoice penalties are capped at AED 5,000 a month, which a large business could almost ignore. The bigger cost is commercial. If your invoices don’t arrive through the system, your customers’ accounts payable teams may not process them , and that delays your cash. The penalty that matters most is the first one. Not having an ASP counts as failing to implement. For Phase 1 businesses, the appointment deadline was 30 October 2026. What to do now Phase 1: confirm your ASP contract is signed and onboarding has started in EmaraTax. Go-live is 1 January 2027. Phase 2: put 31 March 2027 (ASP) and 1 July 2027 (go-live) on the board calendar. Make ASP notification a routine step whenever your licence, address, legal name or other registered details change. Consider going live early. Voluntary e-invoicing can’t be penalised, so it’s a free test run. Sources: Cabinet Decision No. 173 of 2026 on violations and administrative penalties under the e-invoicing legislation (Ministry of Fin What is the penalty for not appointing an e-invoicing ASP? It counts as failing to implement: AED 5,000 for the first instance, then AED 5,000 for each month it continues, capped at AED 50,000 in any 12 months. What is the penalty for not issuing an e-invoice? AED 100 per e-invoice or credit note, capped at AED 5,000 per calendar month. Is voluntary early e-invoicing penalised? No. Mistakes made before your mandatory date don't attract these penalties.

t: Choosing an E-Invoicing Provider (ASP) in the UAE: What to Check Before You Sign
d: How to choose a UAE e-invoicing Accredited Service Provider: the Ministry of Finance's selection criteria, contract points to check, and the onboarding steps.
c: Every business in scope needs an Accredited Service Provider (ASP) : the company that sends, receives and reports your e-invoices. As of 16 November 2026, the Ministry of Finance lists 88 accredited ASPs , and most of them will tell you they’re the right choice. The Ministry has published its own guidance on what to look at. Here it is, turned into questions to ask, plus the contract points it doesn’t cover. The ground rules One ASP, both directions. You appoint a single ASP for sending (sales) and receiving (purchases). You can’t split them. Group companies can differ. Each member of a VAT Tax Group can use a different ASP, but most groups standardise on one. Accredited only. Check the provider is on the Ministry’s list of accredited ASPs , and note its accreditation number. Some providers’ marketing still refers to an earlier “pre-approved” stage. You start onboarding. Onboarding begins from the e-invoicing tile in EmaraTax , not from the ASP’s side. Phase 1 is already late. Businesses with revenue of AED 50 million or more had to appoint by 30 October 2026 . Smaller businesses have until 31 March 2027 . (Which phase are you in? ) Six things the Ministry says to check 1. Experience. How long has it provided e-invoicing, and how long has it been on Peppol? How long has it operated in the UAE, and when was it accredited here? A provider that has run e-invoicing in other countries has already dealt with problems that a new entrant hasn’t met yet. 2. Product. Is the platform its own, or a resold third-party product? Is support in-house or subcontracted? If it’s resold, find out who you call when something breaks at month-end. 3. ERP integration. Does it have a ready connector for your ERP, or will someone build a custom integration? Who does the field mapping, and is that in the price? This is where most projects slip. 4. Security and data. Which certifications does it hold (ISO and others)? How is data encrypted, and what’s its incident response? Where is your data stored , in the UAE or overseas? 5. Support and uptime. What are the response times, and is there an uptime commitment written into the contract? 6. Price. Per-invoice or subscription? Are there set-up, integration or archive fees? The Ministry recommends that contracts include 100 free e-invoices a year . Ask whether yours does. Contract points the guidance doesn’t spell out These come from how the rules work, not from the Ministry’s checklist: Archive and exit. Ministerial Decision No. 197 of 2026 requires you to keep e-invoice data for the full Tax Procedures Law period: generally 5 years , and longer in some cases, such as real estate. You can hand storage to the ASP, but the legal obligation stays with you . The contract should give you full data export in a readable format, during the contract and after it ends. Switching. The guidelines don’t describe a switching process, so put notice periods, data handover and parallel running into the contract yourself. Rejections. Agree in writing who monitors failed invoices, how you’re told, and how fast fixes happen. The 14-business-day issuing deadline doesn’t stop while an invoice sits in an error queue. Data-change notices. Not telling your ASP about changes to your FTA-registered details costs AED 250 a day . Make it part of your licence-renewal checklist. Four steps to go-live The guidelines set out the path: Understand. Confirm your phase and date. List the changes needed in your ERP, billing and approval processes. Select and onboard. Sign with one ASP, onboard through EmaraTax, and get your Peppol Participant Identifier (0235 followed by your TIN). Test. Agree the data format with the ASP, then test sending, receiving and FTA reporting end to end with real invoice scenarios: credit notes, advances, foreign currency, zero-rated sales. Go live. Agree roles for monitoring and error fixing, start exchanging, and keep the ASP updated when your details change. A practical shortlist method Start with 3 providers that a Can I use different e-invoicing providers for sales and purchases? No. You appoint a single ASP for both sending and receiving. Members of a VAT Tax Group can use different ASPs. What should I check before signing with an ASP? Accreditation, experience, whether the platform is its own, your ERP connector, security and data location, support and uptime, total cost, and contract terms for archive export and switching. Who is responsible for keeping e-invoice records? You are. You can hand storage to the ASP, but the obligation to keep the data for the Tax Procedures Law period, generally 5 years, stays with you.

t: How a UAE E-Invoice Actually Travels: The Five-Corner Model in Plain English
d: How a UAE e-invoice moves from your ERP to your customer and the FTA, what your ASP does, what an e-invoice contains, and what to do when a customer isn't ready.
c: From go-live, emailing a PDF doesn’t count as issuing an invoice. The invoice has to travel as structured data through two service providers, with the tax data reported to the FTA on the way. Here’s how that works, based on the Ministry of Finance’s Electronic Invoicing Guidelines v2.0 . The five corners You (the supplier) send the invoice data from your ERP or billing system to your ASP, in a format you’ve agreed with them. Your ASP validates the data and converts it into the UAE standard, PINT-AE XML . It also generates the invoice’s unique ID (UUID). Your ASP sends the invoice over the Peppol network to your customer’s ASP , and at the same time reports the tax data to the FTA . Your customer’s ASP validates the invoice, confirms receipt and delivers it to your customer . The FTA confirms the tax data to both ASPs, and each ASP passes the confirmation back to its client. If the invoice fails validation at your customer’s ASP, that ASP tells your ASP and the FTA. The failure comes back to you to fix. Two things to take from this: You stay responsible. The ASP does the sending, but the guidelines are clear that the obligation remains with the supplier. You calculate every value on the invoice. A wrong VAT figure is your error, not your ASP’s. There’s no PDF and no QR code. The legal e-invoice is the XML. You can still send a PDF copy for convenience, but it doesn’t replace the e-invoice. Your Peppol address Every business on the system gets a Participant Identifier : 0235 followed by its 10-digit TIN , the first 10 digits of its TRN. That’s the address invoices are sent to. Each member of a VAT group has its own TIN and identifier, based on its own TRN, not the group representative’s. What an e-invoice has to contain The Ministry’s mandatory fields list sets out 51 mandatory fields under PINT-AE, plus conditional ones. The data falls into a few groups: Header: invoice number, issue date, invoice type code, currency, due date, UUID. Seller and buyer: name, TRN (or TIN if not VAT-registered), legal registration details and issuing authority, address, electronic address. Lines: item name, quantity, unit of measure, unit price, discounts and charges, VAT category, rate and amount, and whether it’s goods or services. Totals and VAT breakdown: net, VAT and gross totals, amounts already paid, amount payable, and VAT by category. Some points from the clarifications in v2.0: A VAT-registered seller puts its 15-digit TRN in the VAT number field. A seller that isn’t VAT-registered uses its 10-digit TIN in a different field. A Corporate Tax TRN must never go in the VAT field. Advance payments: issue a tax invoice when the advance is received. The final invoice covers only the balance and refers back to the advance invoice. Credit notes: one credit note can cover several invoices, and it can be partial. A negative invoice must be issued as a credit note. Invoice type code 480 is for supplies entirely outside the scope of UAE VAT. HSN codes are optional for now. The Ministry will announce when they become mandatory. You can’t add your own fields to PINT-AE. The practical point: most ERPs don’t capture all of this today , especially buyer legal registration details. That data gap is usually the biggest piece of work in a project, not the connection to the ASP. When your customer isn’t ready Phases go live at different times, so you’ll often be live before some customers are. Your obligation doesn’t depend on theirs. The customer is in scope but not live yet: you still issue the e-invoice through your ASP, using the placeholder endpoint 0235:9900000098 , and the tax data is reported. You also send a normal tax invoice, such as a PDF, so they can recover input VAT. An overseas customer with no Peppol ID: you still issue an e-invoice, using the placeholder endpoint 0235:9900000099 . A consumer: no e-invoice. B2C is outside the system for now. Timing The decisions require e-invoices and credit notes to be issued and transmitted within 14 busine Is a PDF still a valid invoice under UAE e-invoicing? No. The legal e-invoice is the PINT-AE XML sent through your ASP. A PDF can go alongside it as a copy, but it doesn't replace it. What is my Peppol Participant Identifier? 0235 followed by your 10-digit TIN, which is the first 10 digits of your TRN. What if my customer isn't live on e-invoicing yet? You still issue the e-invoice through your ASP to the placeholder endpoint 0235:9900000098, and also send a normal tax invoice such as a PDF.

t: Does UAE E-Invoicing Apply to Your Business? Scope, Exclusions and Your Go-Live Date
d: Who UAE e-invoicing applies to, what is excluded, how the AED 50 million test works, and your deadlines to appoint an ASP and go live, per Guidelines v2.0.
c: The question I hear most about e-invoicing is “does this even apply to us?” Usually it comes from businesses that aren’t VAT registered, or that only invoice group companies. The Ministry of Finance answered most of it in version 2.0 of the UAE Electronic Invoicing Guidelines , published on 26 October 2026. Short answer: if you do business in the UAE, assume you’re in scope until you find a specific exclusion. Who is in scope E-invoicing applies to any person doing business in the UAE, regardless of VAT registration . That’s the point most people miss. A business below the VAT threshold, or one making only exempt supplies, still has to issue e-invoices for its business-to-business sales. A few cases the guidelines settle: Free Zone businesses are not carved out. They follow the same rules as mainland businesses. Holding companies earning only passive income (dividends, interest) with no business transactions are out of scope. But if the holding company recharges costs to subsidiaries or anyone else, such as management fees, those recharges are business transactions and need e-invoices. Non-residents that must issue UAE tax invoices under the VAT law must issue them as e-invoices. Businesses with no VAT registration need a Tax Identification Number (TIN) , the 10-digit number at the start of a TRN. If you’re not registered for any tax, you generate one through EmaraTax. What is excluded Supplies to consumers (B2C) , and sales by individuals who aren’t in business. You keep issuing normal VAT invoices or receipts to consumers. Sovereign government activities that don’t compete with the private sector. International passenger air transport with an electronic ticket, and related services documented on an Electronic Miscellaneous Document. International air cargo with an airway bill, for 24 months. Exempt and zero-rated financial services under Article 42 of the VAT Executive Regulation. Standard-rated financial services to UAE customers stay in scope. Imports of goods and services. Transactions within the same VAT Tax Group , until 31 December 2028. This is the Ministerial Decision No. 197 exclusion , and it covers VAT groups only, not Corporate Tax groups. One trap: the FTA’s existing administrative exceptions for tax invoices (for example, approvals to issue simplified invoices) don’t carry over to e-invoices. Which phase you’re in   Appoint an ASP by Go live by Revenue of AED 50 million or more 30 October 2026 1 January 2027 Revenue under AED 50 million 31 March 2027 1 July 2027 Government entities 31 March 2027 1 October 2027 How revenue is measured. The guidelines define revenue as gross income in your most recent accounting period , based on your financial statements, or other documents acceptable to the FTA if there are none. They don’t say whether revenue is added up across a group, so test each entity on its own figures. If a group member is near the line, get advice rather than guessing. New businesses. A business set up after these dates doesn’t get a grace period. It must appoint an ASP and finish onboarding before it issues its first invoice , and that first invoice must be an e-invoice. Going early. Anyone can start voluntarily before their date. Voluntary e-invoices must meet the full technical rules, but penalties only apply from your mandatory date. If you’re a Phase 1 business The deadline to appoint an ASP was 30 October 2026 , and go-live is about six weeks away. If you haven’t appointed one, that’s the first job this week. Not having an ASP falls within the “failure to implement” penalty, which starts at AED 5,000. What to do now Confirm your phase using revenue in your latest financial statements, entity by entity. Check for exclusions line by line. Most businesses have at least some sales in scope. Get a TIN for any in-scope entity without a TRN. List intra-VAT-group flows separately, since they’re deferred, not exempt. Pick your ASP. Here’s what to check before you sign . Sources: UAE Electronic Invoicing G Does UAE e-invoicing apply if I'm not VAT-registered? Yes. It applies regardless of VAT registration. A business without a TRN needs a 10-digit TIN, generated through EmaraTax. When does UAE e-invoicing start for my business? Revenue of AED 50 million or more: go live by 1 January 2027. Under AED 50 million: appoint an ASP by 31 March 2027 and go live by 1 July 2027. Government entities: 1 October 2027. Are sales to consumers covered by UAE e-invoicing? No. B2C supplies are excluded. You keep issuing normal VAT invoices or receipts to consumers.

t: What Your Auditor Actually Tests in Your VAT Returns
d: The six checks a UAE auditor runs on your VAT position at year end, why each one finds problems, and how to have the answers ready before fieldwork starts.
c: A statutory audit isn’t a VAT audit. But VAT runs through almost every balance an auditor tests: revenue, purchases, payables, cash and provisions. So most year-end audits in the UAE end up looking hard at your VAT position. Below are the six checks that find most of the issues, why each one matters, and what to have ready before fieldwork starts. Why your auditor cares about VAT at all The auditor’s job is to give an opinion on your financial statements. VAT affects them in three ways: The VAT payable or refundable balance is a liability or an asset on your balance sheet. It has to exist, be complete and be correctly valued. Errors in VAT usually mean errors in revenue or expenses. Output VAT that doesn’t match sales often points to sales that are missing or misclassified. Unreported mistakes mean penalties. Under the auditing standards, the auditor has to consider whether you’re complying with laws that affect the financial statements, and whether you need a provision for penalties. The six checks 1. Do the returns agree to the ledger? The auditor adds up output and input VAT from the returns covering your financial year and compares them with the general ledger. Every difference needs an explanation. Some differences are just timing . If your VAT quarters don’t line up with your financial year, a return can straddle the year end. That’s fine as long as you can show it. Others are errors . A common one is VAT booked on an advance payment but left out of the return. Under the VAT Law, the date of supply can be the date the payment is received, so the VAT was due then. That needs a voluntary disclosure and may attract penalties. From my audits: one of the most common differences doesn’t show up in the VAT ledger at all. Bank credits for the year don’t match the revenue reported in the VAT returns. Some of the gap usually has a good reason, such as loans received, capital introduced, transfers between the company’s own accounts, or refunds. Whatever is left after those is revenue the auditor has to chase, and VAT that may be missing from the returns. Run this check yourself before the auditor does. Banks now run it too: see the case of a bank that compared VAT returns with bank credits . 2. Does the VAT control account roll forward? Opening balance, plus net VAT from the returns, less payments to the FTA, should equal the closing balance. That closing balance should then agree with what EmaraTax shows, after any payments made in the last days of the year. When it doesn’t, the usual causes are: an adjustment in a return that was never booked in the ledger, a payment posted to the wrong account, or a penalty paid but never recorded. 3. Is all revenue in the VAT returns? The auditor goes the other way too: from the sales ledger to the returns. Standard-rated sales should carry 5% output VAT. Zero-rated and exempt sales should be identified and explained. Gaps here usually point to revenue recorded outside the main sales cycle, such as other income, asset disposals or recharges to related parties. 4. Is zero-rating supported? Zero-rated exports are where VAT savings turn into exposures. For exports of goods, the Executive Regulation requires official and commercial evidence of export within 90 days of the date of supply. The auditor will sample exports and ask for: customs exit documents, bills of lading or airway bills, and for services, contracts showing where the customer is and where the service is used. If the evidence is missing, the sale may be standard-rated, and the 5% becomes your cost. 5. Is the input VAT recoverable? The auditor samples input VAT and checks for: a valid tax invoice , with the supplier’s TRN verified, business use , and blocked items . Under Article 53 of the Executive Regulation, these include entertainment for people other than employees, motor vehicles available for personal use, and goods or services for employees’ personal use. From 1 October 2026, this check goes further. Under FTA Decision No. 13  Why does a statutory auditor look at VAT? VAT affects the balance sheet, errors in VAT usually mean errors in revenue or expenses, and unreported mistakes may need a provision for penalties. What evidence supports zero-rated exports? Official and commercial evidence of export within 90 days, such as customs exit documents and bills of lading or airway bills. What should I prepare before a VAT-related audit? The returns with a ledger reconciliation, a control account roll-forward agreed to EmaraTax, an export evidence file, a list of blocked input VAT, and the year's FTA correspondence.

t: Five Changes to the UAE E-Invoicing Rules, and the One Most Groups Will Misread
d: What Ministerial Decision No. 197 of 2026 changed in UAE e-invoicing: the 24-month Tax Group exclusion, 14 business days, data storage and system failures.
c: Six weeks before mandatory e-invoicing starts, the Ministry of Finance has changed some of the rules. Ministerial Decision No. 197 of 2026 amends Ministerial Decision No. 243 of 2025, the main e-invoicing decision. It has been in force since 1 October 2026 and was announced on 19 October. Most of it makes life easier. One part, the new Tax Group exclusion, is narrower than the headlines suggest. The five changes at a glance Tax Group exclusion (new). Transactions between members of the same Tax Group are Excluded Transactions for 24 months from 1 January 2027 . Deadline to issue and transmit. E-invoices and e-credit notes must be issued and transmitted through the system within 14 Business Days from the Date of Business Transaction. This is subject to Clause 4 of Article 6. Data storage. The new Article 11 only requires you to keep e-invoices, credit notes and related data for the period set in the Tax Procedures Law , and to be able to produce them to the FTA on request. It says nothing about where the data must be kept. Ministry and press coverage say the earlier rule required storage within the UAE. System Failure. Article 12 is repealed and the “System Failure” definition deleted. That removes the requirement, reported in the coverage, to notify the FTA of a system failure within two business days. Accredited Service Provider. Accreditation is now defined by reference to “the legislation regulating the Electronic Invoicing System” in general, rather than one specific decision. The decision also adds two definitions, Tax Group and Taxable Person , both tied to the VAT Law. The first is the one that matters. The exclusion follows the VAT group, not the Corporate Tax group The decision defines a Tax Group as “two or more Persons registered with the Authority for Tax purposes as a single Taxable Person in accordance with the provisions of the VAT Law.” That’s a VAT group. A Corporate Tax Group is a separate registration with separate conditions (see what a Corporate Tax Group is ). Many groups have one and not the other. So: A and B are in the same VAT Tax Group: invoices between them are excluded until 31 December 2028. A and C are in a Corporate Tax Group but not a VAT group: their invoices are in scope from go-live. A invoices a related company outside its VAT group, or any outside customer: in scope , on the normal timeline. If your ERP project team has been told “intra-group is out”, check which group they mean. It’s a deferral, not an exemption The exclusion runs for 24 months from 1 January 2027 , whatever your go-live date. Intra-VAT-group transactions come into scope on 1 January 2029 . For a business with revenue of AED 50 million or more, that’s two years after its own go-live. A smaller business that goes live on 1 July 2027 gets 18 months. Two practical points: Build the logic now. Your ERP needs to flag intra-VAT-group invoices and route them differently. If that flag can be switched off in 2029, the change is configuration, not a new project. You can opt in. Clause 3 of the new Article 4 lets you issue and exchange e-invoices voluntarily for Excluded Transactions. If you do, the rules apply to you in full, except the penalty provisions . That makes it a low-risk way to test intra-group invoicing before it becomes mandatory. The other changes, in practice The 14-business-day deadline. Count it in business days and build it into your billing cut-off. Clause 4 of Article 6 still applies, so where the VAT Law has its own timing rules, check those too. Don’t treat 14 business days as a blanket extension. Storage. Moving your e-invoice archive outside the UAE no longer seems to break a location rule. The obligation now is retention and production : keep the data for the full Tax Procedures Law period and make sure you can hand it over when the FTA asks. If your provider or ERP host is overseas, check your contract gives you guaranteed access and export of the data for that whole period. System failures. There’s no lon Are intra-group invoices excluded from UAE e-invoicing? Only between members of the same VAT Tax Group, and only until 31 December 2028. Transactions within a Corporate Tax Group that isn't a VAT group are in scope. How long do I have to issue a UAE e-invoice? Within 14 business days of the transaction, subject to the VAT Law's own timing rules. Do e-invoices have to be stored in the UAE? Decision No. 197 only requires you to keep them for the Tax Procedures Law period and produce them on request. It says nothing about location.

t: If It Isn't Documented, It Didn't Happen: Protecting Your Input VAT Under Decision No. 13
d: The evidence file and written verification policy FTA Decision No. 13 of 2026 requires, FTA Example 8, and a 6-step plan to protect your input VAT.
c: Parts 2 , 3 and 4 covered the checks. This part covers the thing that makes them count: proof . A check you did but can’t show is, for the FTA’s purposes, a check you didn’t do. Why bother: FTA Example 8 Example 8 is the FTA’s positive case: The business applied all the Decision No. 13 measures and kept the documentary evidence. The FTA later establishes tax evasion elsewhere in the supply chain . The business took no part in the evasion and did not know of it . It is treated as unaware , and the normal input tax recovery rules apply. The input tax stands. Same evasion in the chain as the businesses that lost. The difference is the file. Documented checks turn a supplier’s fraud into their problem, not yours. All eight FTA examples, side by side Look at the four that lost: no ID, an ignored red flag, no reason for foreign accounts, an unquestioned price. None of them needed expensive tools. Every one could have been avoided with a few minutes of checking and a note on file. What goes in the file Evidence file, per supplier and supply (Article 5(3)) ID copies and trade licence or registry extract Place of business proof: map capture or visit note Risk review, with explanations for any flags Bank letter and reputation review (over AED 375,000) Supply assessment: price, scope, origin, payment Written verification policy (Article 5(4)) Names who implements, reviews and supervises the checks States their powers and responsibilities clearly Kept at the designated location for tax records Lets the FTA confirm the steps were done correctly Free template: a ready-to-edit Supplier Verification Policy in Word , covering roles, tiers, checks, escalation and records. The policy is easy to skip because it feels like paperwork. Don’t skip it. It’s what turns “our accountant usually checks” into a control the FTA can rely on. Your 6-step action plan Clean the supplier master. Collect missing licences, IDs, TRNs and addresses. Segment by spend. Tag every supplier against the AED 10,000, 100,000 and 375,000 tests (see Part 3). Build one checklist. A single onboarding form covering identity, premises and risk flags. Add payment controls. Block third-party and foreign payees unless there is a documented reason. Approve the policy. Name owners, reviewers and supervisors; set the record location. Train and re-verify. Brief procurement and finance; diarise annual reviews. Free tool: the Supplier Verification tool covers steps 2 and 3: it tiers your suppliers by spend, runs the checklist and red flags for each one, and produces a record you can sign and file. Most businesses can finish steps 1 to 3 in a few weeks. If you’re also preparing for e-invoicing, run both projects together: they touch the same vendor master, so you only clean it once. The series in one paragraph A valid tax invoice no longer guarantees input VAT recovery. If the FTA establishes evasion in your supply chain, you keep your claim only if you can show you verified the supplier (identity, premises, red flags, plus bank and reputation over AED 375,000) and the supply (reason, payment, price, licence, origin), at the depth your spend requires, and documented all of it under a written policy. Do that, and you’re Example 8. Skip it, and you’re one of the other four. What does FTA Example 8 show? A business that applied all the Decision No. 13 checks and kept the evidence was treated as unaware of evasion elsewhere in its chain, so its input VAT stood. Do I need a written supplier verification policy? Yes. Article 5(4) expects a written policy naming who implements, reviews and supervises the checks, kept where tax records are kept. What goes in a supplier evidence file? ID and licence copies, place of business proof, the risk review, a bank letter and reputation review above AED 375,000, and the supply assessment of price, scope, origin and payment.

t: Too Cheap, Wrong Licence, Odd Bank Account: 4 Red Flags That Can Cost You Input VAT
d: Four transaction red flags that can cost you input VAT under FTA Decision No. 13 of 2026: payment, price, licence scope and goods origin (FTA Examples 4 to 7).
c: A supplier can pass every identity check in Part 2 and still be part of an evasion chain. That is why Article 4 of Decision No. 13 shifts the focus from who you buy from to what you are buying, and how you pay . There are six supply checks: Commercial reason: the supplier’s involvement rests on genuine commercial reasons. Payment conditions: the method and terms make commercial sense. Electronic payment is the default. Price and margin: not unjustifiably far from market without a clear reason. Licence scope: what you buy falls within the supplier’s ordinary or licensed activity. Goods origin: authenticity, origin, and the supplier’s right to sell the goods. Intermediaries: a clear, justified commercial reason for any middleman’s role. The FTA illustrates four of these with worked examples. Two businesses lost; two got it right. Red flag 1: the payment doesn’t make sense (Example 4) A bakery orders furniture worth AED 60,000 (including VAT) from one manufacturer. It is billed as three AED 20,000 invoices from three different companies , each naming a different foreign bank account . The reason given: “convenience” . The owner accepts it. Result: should have been aware . There was no commercial reason for third parties or foreign accounts, under Article 4(2). The payment rules in plain terms: Pay electronically. This is the expected default. Cash only with a reason: documented, easy to verify, and within limits still to be set by a Minister of Finance decision. Those limits haven’t been published yet. Third parties or foreign accounts need a reasonable commercial explanation that fits the evidence you hold. Accounts payable is your last line of defence. A change of payee, a foreign account or a split invoice should trigger a documented query before payment, not after. Red flag 2: the price is too good (Example 5) A hotel needs 200 branded bed sheet sets . The wholesale market price is AED 400 to 800 per set . A new wholesaler offers AED 200 . The hotel accepts without question. Result: should have been aware . The price wasn’t checked against the market, under Article 4(3)(a). Half the bottom of the market range is not a bargain. It’s a flag. A big discount can be legitimate (clearance stock, a closing business), but you need that reason in writing, before you buy . Checks that worked: licence scope and goods origin (Examples 6 and 7) Example 6: the restaurant. A new wholesaler offers to sell shishas. The restaurant checks the trade licence. It covers consulting, IT and marketing only . The restaurant declines. Result: the check worked. Licence scope verified under Article 4(3)(b). A two-minute licence check stopped a bad purchase. Example 7: the clinic. The clinic’s usual wholesaler imports three aesthetic devices . The clinic collects serial numbers and customs documents , and still reviews the supplier’s licences every year . Result: requirement met. Goods origin verified under Article 4(3)(c). Even a long-standing supplier gets re-checked. Your supply checklist (copy this) For every taxable supply above the small-supply threshold: Why this supplier? Commercial reason noted Paid electronically to an account in the supplier’s own name. If not: written reason Price compared with market (two quotes, a price list or a past purchase). If far off: written reason Goods or services fall within the supplier’s licensed activity For goods: origin evidence kept (serial numbers, customs documents, distributor authorisation) Any intermediary: their role and why it’s needed, in writing Next, Part 5 : the final piece. If none of this is documented, none of it happened. The evidence file, the written policy, FTA Example 8 and a 6-step plan to get compliant. Can I pay a UAE supplier's invoice into a foreign or third-party bank account? Only with a reasonable commercial explanation that fits your evidence. In FTA Example 4, accepting 'convenience' as the reason meant the buyer should have been aware. Is a very low price a VAT red flag? Yes. In FTA Example 5, a hotel paid half the bottom of the market range without checking, and should have been aware. A real discount needs a written reason before you buy. Why check the supplier's trade licence? The goods or services must fall within the supplier's licensed activity. In FTA Example 6, a licence for consulting and IT only showed the supplier couldn't sell shishas.

t: AED 10K, 100K, 375K: The Three Numbers That Decide How Deep You Verify Suppliers
d: How spend per supplier sets the depth of your input VAT checks under FTA Decision No. 13 of 2026, why splitting invoices fails, and when to re-verify.
c: Part 2 covered what to check about a supplier. This part covers how deep you need to go, and how often . The answer comes down to three numbers. Get them wrong and you either over-check every AED 300 stationery order, or under-check the supplier who actually matters. The three tiers Under AED 10,000 per supply (excluding VAT) The checks may be skipped. But not if the total spend with that supplier exceeds AED 100,000 in the past 12 months or the next 12 months. Standard: all other supplies Full supplier checks (identity, place of business, risk indicators) plus supply checks (commercial reason, payment, price, licence scope, goods origin). We cover the supply checks in Part 4. Over AED 375,000 with the same supplier (past or next 12 months) Everything above, plus : a written confirmation of the supplier’s UAE bank account (for example, an IBAN letter), and a review of public reviews and media coverage of the supplier. The key word in all three: supplier . The tests look at cumulative spend per supplier, not the size of an individual invoice. Why splitting invoices doesn’t help Here is an illustrative example. You use a cleaning contractor at AED 9,500 a month . Every single invoice is under AED 10,000, so it looks like the small-supply relief applies. It doesn’t, for two reasons: Backward-looking: by month 11, total spend is AED 104,500. You are over AED 100,000 in the past 12 months, so the relief is gone. Forward-looking: the test also covers the next 12 months. If you signed a 12-month contract you already know is worth AED 114,000, the relief is lost from the first invoice . The same forward-looking logic applies at AED 375,000. An expected contract value counts. If you’re about to sign a AED 400,000 annual fit-out or IT contract, the bank letter and reputation review belong in onboarding, not in month nine. Practical takeaway: your AP system needs a running 12-month spend total per supplier, plus a flag for known contract values. Invoice-level controls won’t catch this. When to verify: four triggers First dealing: verify the supplier before the first VAT-able supply. Every supply: verify each taxable supply you receive or accept. Every 12 months: re-verify recurring suppliers who haven’t been checked in the past 12 months. Continuously: monitor cumulative spend against the AED 100,000 and AED 375,000 tests. The trap is trigger 3. Long-standing suppliers feel safe, so nobody re-checks them. The FTA’s own Example 7 (Part 4) shows a clinic reviewing its usual wholesaler’s licence every year. Familiarity is not verification. Set it up in your books If you run Tally or any ERP, three fields on the vendor master do most of the work: Field What it does Spend tier (Under 10K / Standard / Over 375K) Tells AP which checks must be on file Last verified date Drives the 12-month re-verification Expected 12-month contract value Catches the forward-looking test before the first invoice Run a monthly report on rolling 12-month spend per supplier and review anyone who crossed AED 100,000 or AED 375,000 since last month. Free tool: the Supplier Verification tool does the tiering for you: paste your supplier list from Excel and it sorts each supplier into the right tier. Next, Part 4 : the supplier checks out. Now, is the transaction itself genuine? Four red flags from FTA Examples 4 to 7. Can I skip supplier checks on invoices under AED 10,000? Only if total spend with that supplier doesn't exceed AED 100,000 in the past 12 months or the next 12 months. The test is per supplier, not per invoice. Does splitting invoices avoid the verification thresholds? No. The thresholds look at cumulative spend per supplier, backward and forward, including known contract values. How often must suppliers be re-verified? Before the first supply, for each taxable supply, and again for recurring suppliers not checked in the past 12 months.

t: Who Are You Actually Buying From? The Supplier Checks the FTA Now Expects
d: The supplier checks under FTA Decision No. 13 of 2026: identity, place of business and three red flags, explained through FTA Examples 1, 2 and 3.
c: In Part 1 we saw that your input VAT is now only as clean as your supplier. So the obvious next question: how well do you actually know your suppliers? For many SMEs, the honest answer is “a phone number and a TRN.” Article 3 of Decision No. 13 asks for three things more. Check 1: Who are they? What you need depends on whether the supplier is an individual or a company. Individual supplier (natural person) A copy of a valid ID: Emirates ID or passport. Meet them before any VAT-able supply : in person, by phone or by video call. Company supplier (legal person) Verify incorporation using official databases (for example, the ADGM or DIFC registries), or the certificate of incorporation or trade licence. The details must be valid and match the name, address and employees. A valid ID for the director, agent or authorised employee you deal with. The common SME gap is freelancers and small contractors sourced online, with no ID on file. A two-minute video call and an ID copy closes it. Check 2: Do they actually exist somewhere? This applies to individuals and companies alike. Confirm there is a real place of business , using map and navigation platforms or a site visit. It must also fit the activity : a machinery supplier should have a yard or warehouse, not a desk in a shared office. FTA Examples 1 and 2: same question, opposite outcomes Example 1: the boutique. A boutique opening a new branch finds a curtain specialist through social media ads. All communication happens on WhatsApp. The supplier’s identity is never verified. The job is billed at AED 10,000 + AED 500 VAT for measuring, tailoring and installing. Result: if evasion is established, the boutique should have been aware . Identity was never verified under Article 3(1). Note that the job was not below AED 10,000, so the small-supply exception (Part 3) didn’t help. Example 2: the construction firm. A construction company needs light machinery and contacts a newly registered industrial supplier. Its representatives visit the supplier’s warehouse in Al Quoz Industrial Area and evaluate the equipment before completing the purchase. Result: the place of business check is met under Article 3(2). A real warehouse that fits a machinery business. The difference isn’t the size of the business or the deal. It’s that one buyer looked and the other didn’t. Check 3: Any red flags? Decision No. 13 lists three risk indicators. Any one of them counts as a flag: The supplier’s address changed more than twice in the last 12 months. Key employees or managers changed more than twice in the last 12 months. The deal is disproportionate to the supplier’s size or track record . A flag is not an automatic disqualification. It means you need a clear, justified explanation that is consistent with the evidence you hold, kept on file and ready to give the FTA on request. FTA Example 3: the flag that was ignored A large warehouse needs a new ERP system for real-time inventory and delivery insight. A startup software firm says it has a team of 25 experienced consultants and can go live in 4 weeks . The startup’s own website shows 3 employees , with experience only in mobile apps . The warehouse signs anyway, because of the promised speed: AED 20,000 + AED 1,000 VAT. Result: if evasion is established, the warehouse should have been aware . The disproportionate-transaction indicator under Article 3(3)(a)(3) was visible from public information. Three lessons: The mismatch was on the supplier’s own website .
