That is exactly the kind of check the FTA expects you to do. Speed or price is not a commercial justification. Finding a flag is fine. Proceeding without a documented explanation is the problem. Either write down a credible reason, or walk away. Your supplier checklist (copy this) For every new supplier, before the first VAT-able supply: ID copy (individual) or registry extract / trade licence + authorised person’s ID (company) Name, address and people match across documents Place of business confirmed b What supplier checks does FTA Decision No. 13 require? Identity, a real place of business that fits the activity, and three risk indicators. Over AED 375,000 of spend you also need a bank account letter and a reputation review. Is a red flag an automatic reason to stop buying from a supplier? No. A flag needs a clear, documented explanation consistent with your evidence. Proceeding without one is the problem. Is checking the supplier's TRN enough? No. The FTA expects identity, place of business and risk checks as well, all documented before the first VAT-able supply.

t: Your Tax Invoice Won't Save Your Input VAT Anymore
d: Since 1 October 2026 a valid tax invoice no longer guarantees input VAT recovery. What FTA Decision No. 13 of 2026 changed and the test that decides your claim.
c: For years, the input VAT conversation in the UAE was simple: get a valid tax invoice, make sure the supplier’s TRN is right, claim it. That is no longer the whole story. Since 1 October 2026 , holding a valid tax invoice is the starting point for recovering input VAT. It is not the finish line. This is Part 1 of a 5-part series on FTA Decision No. 13 of 2026 and the FTA’s Public Clarification VATP048 . By the end of the series you will know every check the FTA expects, all eight worked examples it published, and what to do about it this quarter. What changed Two pieces fit together: Article 54(bis)(2) of the VAT Law lets the FTA reject your input tax if the supply was part of a supply, or a chain of supplies, linked to tax evasion . This applies even if you were not involved, as long as you “should have been aware” of the link. Decision No. 13 of 2026 (issued 22 July 2026, in force 1 October 2026) sets out the checks that let you prove you were not aware, and could not have been. VATP048 then explains how the FTA will apply those checks, using eight worked examples. We go through all eight in this series. The one-line version: your input VAT claim is now only as clean as your supplier. The test that decides your claim Strip away the legal language and the logic is a single question. If the FTA establishes tax evasion somewhere in your supply chain, did you follow the Decision No. 13 checks and keep the evidence? Yes: you are treated as unaware. The normal input tax rules apply. This is exactly FTA Example 8, which we cover in Part 5. No: your ability to prove you were unaware is weak, and your input tax can be rejected. The checks are your evidence. Without them, you are defending your claim from memory, and memory doesn’t hold up well in a tax audit. Who has to prove what This part is often misunderstood, in both directions. The FTA carries the burden of proving tax evasion (Article 51 of the Tax Procedures Law). It can’t reject your claim just because a supplier looks odd. You carry the burden of proving your verification. Once evasion is established, it’s on you to show what checks you ran. And one more nuance: the checks are not mandatory for every purchase. VATP048 says you don’t need to apply them to all supplies. The Decision only matters where the FTA has established evasion. That sounds like relief. It isn’t. You can’t know in advance which of your suppliers will turn out to be part of an evasion chain. The only workable approach is to build the checks into normal purchasing, so the evidence already exists when you need it. What the checks look like Decision No. 13 has three pillars: Verify the supplier (Article 3): identity, place of business, risk indicators, plus a bank account and reputation check for large spend. Verify the supply (Article 4): genuine commercial reason, payment conditions, price, licence scope, origin of goods, any intermediary’s role. Document it (Article 5): record every step, keep the supporting documents, and keep a written policy naming who runs the checks. The rest of the series takes each pillar apart, with the FTA’s own examples: Part 2: Who are you actually buying from? (supplier checks, Examples 1 to 3) Part 3: AED 10K, 100K, 375K: the numbers that set your checks Part 4: Too cheap, wrong licence, odd bank account (Examples 4 to 7) Part 5: If it isn’t documented, it didn’t happen (Example 8 and a 6-step action plan) What to do this week Pull your top 20 suppliers by spend for the last 12 months. For each one, ask a single question: if the FTA asked me today how I verified this supplier, what would I show them? If the honest answer is “the tax invoice,” you have found your gap. Free tool: the Supplier Verification tool tiers your supplier list by spend and builds a signed evidence record for each supplier. Is a valid tax invoice enough to recover input VAT in the UAE? Not since 1 October 2026. If the FTA establishes evasion in your supply chain, you also need to show you ran the Decision No. 13 checks and kept the evidence. Are the Decision No. 13 checks mandatory for every purchase? No. VATP048 says they don't have to be applied to every supply. They matter where the FTA establishes evasion, and you can't know in advance which supplier that will be. Who has to prove what under Decision No. 13? The FTA must prove tax evasion. Once it does, you must prove the verification checks you ran.

t: Losses, Interest and Reliefs in a UAE Tax Group: What's Shared and What's Ring-Fenced
d: How UAE Tax Groups handle pre-Grouping losses, restricted losses, the interest limit, Small Business Relief and loss transfers, with FTA Examples 22, 36 and 39.
c: Pooling profits and losses is the main reason most groups form a Tax Group (Part 1 ). But not every loss pools. Losses brought in from before the group, and a group’s existing losses when a new member joins, are ring-fenced. Handle them wrong and they’re forfeited. This is the final part of the series. What’s shared and what’s ring-fenced Applied to the group as a whole: Current-year results. One member’s loss offsets another’s profit automatically. The 0% band. The group gets one AED 375,000 band, however many members it has. Small Business Relief. Available only if the group’s combined revenue is AED 3 million or less in the current and every previous Tax Period, and no member belongs to a large multinational group that has to file Country-by-Country Reports. The interest limit. If net interest expense goes over AED 12 million, the deduction is capped at the higher of 30% of the group’s EBITDA or AED 12 million. One highly geared member can shelter behind the others’ EBITDA. The flip side is that a member with enough EBITDA on its own can still be restricted if the group as a whole doesn’t have enough. Participation Exemption thresholds. The 5% holding and AED 4 million cost tests are met by combining holdings across members, and across their Qualifying Group. Ring-fenced: Pre-Grouping Tax Losses , meaning a member’s losses from before it joined. Restricted losses : the group’s own losses when a new member joins. Pre-Grouping interest carried forward. Using a member’s pre-Grouping loss To use a member’s old losses, the group has to work out the Taxable Income attributable to that member , as if it were filing alone. The loss can only be set against that income, and the usual 75% cap applies to the group’s Taxable Income. In FTA Example 36 : J brings a pre-Grouping loss of AED 1m . The group’s 2025 Taxable Income is AED 0.8m , and the income attributable to J is AED 1.2m. The usable amount is the lower of 75% × 0.8m = AED 0.6m and J’s AED 1.2m. So the group uses AED 0.6m and carries AED 0.4m forward. Pre-Grouping losses are used before the group’s own losses, and transferred-in losses come last. Use it or lose it. If the group has room to use a member’s pre-Grouping loss but doesn’t attribute income to that member, the whole pre-Grouping loss is forfeited (Example 37). The same applies to pre-Grouping interest. When a new member joins a group that has losses The group’s existing losses become restricted . They can’t be used against income that belongs to the newcomer. In FTA Example 39 : The group has a 2024 loss of AED 2m . S and T join on 1 January 2025, and S brings its own AED 0.6m pre-Grouping loss. 2025 group income is AED 1.6m . S’s AED 0.6m is used first, which leaves AED 1.0m. The income attributable to the newcomers is S’s AED 1.0m less T’s AED 0.5m loss, so AED 0.5m . The restricted group loss can be used against at most 75% × (AED 1.0m − AED 0.5m) = AED 0.375m in 2025. The unused balance carries forward. The 50% ownership test is applied at the Parent Losses carry forward only if the same owners keep at least 50% of the business, or the same or a similar business continues. For a Tax Group, the test is applied to who owns the Parent Company . In Example 24, one shareholder holds 54% of the members through direct stakes (49% of the Parent plus 5% of the Subsidiary), but the other 51% of the Parent’s shares change hands. That’s a change of more than 50% at the Parent, so the ownership test fails. The business continuity test then has to be met instead. On the other hand, members joining or leaving doesn’t by itself fail the ownership test. Transferring a loss between two Tax Groups A Tax Group can transfer losses to another Taxable Person, including another Tax Group, if there’s 75% common ownership . That’s measured from one group’s Parent through to the other group’s Parent: Example 22: A owns 100% of B, B owns 100% of C, and C owns 80% of X, the Parent of Group 2. 100% × 80% = 80% , so the loss can be transferred Can a Tax Group use a new member's losses from before it joined? Only against Taxable Income attributable to that member, worked out as if it filed alone, and subject to the 75% cap on the group's Taxable Income. Can pre-Grouping losses be forfeited? Yes. If the group has room to use a member's pre-Grouping loss but doesn't attribute income to that member, the whole loss is forfeited (FTA Example 37). Can a Tax Group get Small Business Relief? Only if the group's combined revenue is AED 3 million or less in the current and every previous Tax Period, and no member belongs to a multinational group that files Country-by-Country Reports.

t: The 2-Year Clawback: Moving Assets Inside a UAE Tax Group
d: Asset transfers inside a UAE Tax Group are tax-free until a party leaves within 2 years. How the clawback works, and the elections that follow you out.
c: Inside a Tax Group, moving an asset from one company to another has no tax effect. The gain is eliminated on aggregation (Part 4 ). That makes restructuring cheap, but only as long as both companies stay in the group. This is Part 5. The rule If either the transferor or the transferee leaves the group within 2 years of an intra-group transfer, the gain or loss that was eliminated is brought back into tax . It’s measured at market value at the date of the transfer and taxed in the group on the date the company leaves. The exception: no clawback if the gain would have been exempt or left out of tax anyway, for example under Qualifying Group Relief, Business Restructuring Relief or the Participation Exemption, and that relief wouldn’t itself have been clawed back. FTA Example 20, step by step T, U and W are in a Tax Group. The asset has a book value of AED 1m throughout. 31 March 2024: T transfers the asset to U (market value AED 1.2m). Eliminated. 31 March 2025: U transfers it to W (market value AED 1.4m). Eliminated. 1 February 2027: T sells U to a third party. U is out of the group from 1 January 2027 (Part 3 ). The result: 2024 transfer: U left more than 2 years after it. No clawback. 2025 transfer: U left within 2 years. Qualifying Group Relief wouldn’t have saved it, because U leaving the group within 2 years would have triggered that clawback too. Business Restructuring Relief didn’t fit either: the transfer was for cash and U didn’t cease to exist. So a gain of AED 0.4m (AED 1.4m − AED 1m) is taxed in the group’s 2027 return, and the asset’s tax cost steps up to AED 1.4m . The later market value applies, not the original AED 1.2m, because the 2025 transfer is the one being clawed back. Note too that leaving from 1 January 2027 put U inside the 2-year window, even though the sale happened in February. Mergers inside the group When a member merges into another member and ceases to exist, it leaves the group on that date. FTA Example 13 shows two things: The merger itself: if it meets the conditions for Business Restructuring Relief, the merger gain isn’t taxed. Earlier transfers: X had transferred an asset to Y a year earlier. X then leaving within 2 years would have clawed back Qualifying Group Relief, so that earlier gain is taxed, at its market value at the transfer date. Leaving? You take the group’s values with you In FTA Example 14 , A sells B a non-depreciable asset for AED 120 when its book value is AED 100. In the Aggregated FS the gain is eliminated and the asset stays at AED 100 . B leaves after 2 years: B has to use AED 100 as the asset’s tax value, even though its own books say 120. If B later sells it, the taxable gain is measured from 100. B leaves within 2 years: the AED 20 gain is clawed back into the group’s income, and B’s tax cost steps up to AED 120 . Decisions that follow a company out of the group Once a company joins, the group’s choices become its choices, including after it leaves : Accounting basis: cash or accrual, as the group applied it. Realisation basis election: the company follows whatever the group decided, even if it had made the opposite choice before joining. Investment property depreciation: the group’s election (or non-election) for the 4% annual tax depreciation on fair-valued investment properties applies to the joining company’s properties too, and stays with them. Transitional rule elections: if the group made them, they keep applying to former members. Qualifying Group Relief: if any member has elected it, the whole group is treated as electing, and the election stays with members after they leave. Before you move assets around Keep an intra-group transfer register : date, asset, market value, transferor and transferee. Check the register before any sale of a member or exit from the group. Anything moved in the last 2 years is a possible tax charge. Where you can, structure transfers so that Qualifying Group Relief or Business Restructuring Relief would apply on their own terms.  When is a gain on an intra-group asset transfer clawed back? When either company leaves the Tax Group within 2 years of the transfer. The gain is measured at market value at the transfer date and taxed in the group on the date the company leaves. Can relief switch off the 2-year clawback? Yes, if the gain would have been exempt anyway under Qualifying Group Relief, Business Restructuring Relief or the Participation Exemption, and that relief wouldn't itself have been clawed back. What tax value does an asset have when its owner leaves the group? The value in the group's Aggregated Financial Statements. If the clawback applies, the tax cost steps up to the market value at the transfer date.

t: Aggregated Financial Statements: How a UAE Tax Group's Taxable Income Is Built
d: How to prepare Aggregated Financial Statements for a UAE Corporate Tax Group: what is eliminated, what isn't, and how they differ from an IFRS consolidation.
c: A Tax Group has one Taxable Income, and it starts from one number: the profit in the group’s Aggregated Financial Statements . These aren’t the consolidated accounts most groups already prepare. Getting the difference wrong changes the tax. This is Part 4. Parts 2 and 3 covered who’s in the group; this part covers how their results are combined. How they’re built The framework comes from FTA Decision No. 7 of 2025 and Ministerial Decision No. 84 of 2025. In practice: Start from each member’s own statements (IFRS or IFRS for SMEs), not the consolidation. Align them: same year-end, the Parent’s accounting policies applied throughout, presented in AED . Take pre-tax profit. Corporate Tax balances, current and deferred, are left out. Foreign taxes and other non-Corporate Tax taxes stay in. Add the statements up line by line. Eliminate transactions between members: intra-group balances, income, expenses and unrealised gains. Dividends paid between members drop out as well. Get a special purpose audit and submit it to the FTA within 9 months of the year end. The members’ own statements don’t need auditing for Corporate Tax purposes. A worked example In FTA Example 17 , J owns 100% of K and lends it AED 10m: The AED 10m loan is eliminated on both sides. J’s AED 5m investment in K is kept , and so is K’s equity. Aggregated total assets come to AED 30m and equity to AED 20m, which includes K’s equity held by J. Keeping both the investment and the equity grosses up the balance sheet. That’s deliberate: it keeps goodwill and acquisition fair-value adjustments out of the tax base. Example 18 follows on. If J impairs the AED 10m loan to K, that impairment is eliminated too . A loan write-off between members doesn’t reduce the group’s tax. Aggregated is not consolidated In short: only Tax Group members go in, goodwill and fair value uplifts from buying a company are left out, the investment and the subsidiary’s equity are both kept, an impairment of an investment in a member is not eliminated, and non-member subsidiaries and associates are carried at cost less impairment. One exception: if a member buys a business , meaning assets rather than shares in a company, the resulting goodwill and fair values are in that member’s own books, so they are aggregated (Example 16). If you have subsidiaries that aren’t in the Tax Group, like a QFZP or a foreign company, transactions with them are not eliminated and their accounts are not added in. The exception for losses claimed before joining Normally every intra-group transaction is eliminated. But if a member deducted a loss before joining the group , for example by impairing a loan to another member, then a later reversal of that loss isn’t eliminated. It’s taxed in the group, up to the amount originally deducted. This works one way only. Further impairments after joining are still eliminated and give no deduction. Only the reversal of the earlier deduction is taxed. Other points that change the number Subsidiaries with minority shareholders. All of the subsidiary’s income goes into the group’s Taxable Income, not just the Parent’s share. Deductible expenses are judged across the group. A cost one member incurs for another member’s business can be deductible. A cost incurred for a non-member’s business, like a foreign parent’s, isn’t. Disclosures. The statements must state the special purpose framework, list each member with the Parent’s percentage of share capital, voting rights and profit and net asset entitlement, and show comparatives from the group’s second year onwards. What to do this quarter If you’re in a group, or planning one, set up a separate aggregation workbook next to your consolidation. It should start from members’ standalone pre-tax figures, not the consolidated pack, and keep an elimination schedule that the auditor can trace line by line. Next, Part 5 : moving assets between members is tax-free, until someone leaves within 2 years. Are Aggregated Financial Statements the same as consolidated accounts? No. Only Tax Group members are included, goodwill and fair value uplifts from buying a company are left out, and the Parent's investment and the subsidiary's equity are both kept. Do Aggregated Financial Statements need to be audited? Yes. They need a special purpose audit and must be submitted to the FTA within 9 months of the year end. The members' own statements don't need auditing for Corporate Tax purposes. Is an impairment of a loan to another group member deductible? No. An impairment between members is eliminated on aggregation, so it doesn't reduce the group's tax (FTA Example 18).

t: Joining, Leaving or Closing a UAE Tax Group: The Timing Rules That Catch Groups Out
d: When changes to a UAE Corporate Tax Group take effect, the 20-business-day notification rule, and why a 7-day share transfer can cost a company a whole year.
c: Groups change. Companies are bought, sold, merged and set up. Under the Tax Group rules, when a change takes effect is often more surprising than the change itself. This is Part 3. Part 2 covered the conditions; this part covers what happens when they stop being met. The core rule: whole periods, not days A company has to meet every condition continuously throughout the Tax Period . There’s no apportionment. If it fails for part of a year, it’s treated as outside the group for the whole year. FTA Example 12. T (the Parent) owns 100% of U. On 1 October 2025, T transfers 10% of U to a third party, and on 8 October buys it back. For seven days, T’s stake was 90%. The result: U is out of the group from 1 January 2025 . U files its own 2025 Tax Return and pays its own tax. T has to notify the FTA within 20 business days of 1 October , the day the condition failed. The lesson: run any share movement involving a group member past the tax team first. That includes “temporary” transfers, nominee changes and new share issues. When each change takes effect Forming, joining, leaving or closing by application: apply through EmaraTax before the end of the Tax Period you want the change to apply to. It takes effect from the start of that period, or from another period the FTA decides on. A newly incorporated company can join from its incorporation date , as long as its first year-end matches the group’s. In Example 11, a subsidiary set up on 15 September 2024 joins from that date. It doesn’t have to wait until 1 January 2025. A member that fails a condition is out from the start of that Tax Period, and the FTA must be notified within 20 business days . A member that merges into another member stays in the group until the date it ceases to exist. FTA approval also isn’t a permanent green light. If the conditions aren’t met throughout the group’s first period, the FTA treats the group, or that member, as never having been formed for that period, even though it approved the application. Selling a subsidiary When a member is sold to a buyer outside the group: it leaves from the start of the Tax Period in which the sale happens, and so do any subsidiaries below it, the buyer can’t group with it for that period either, because neither side owned it for the whole year. On timing: for the share capital test, the seller remains the owner until legal title passes . Signing the share purchase agreement isn’t enough. For the profits and net assets test, the buyer is generally treated as entitled once the agreement becomes unconditional . When the Parent Company changes A group can carry on under a new Parent Company in two situations: the new Parent meets all the conditions in relation to the old Parent, for example a holding company above it that becomes eligible, or the old Parent ceases to exist and the new Parent, or a Subsidiary, is its universal legal successor (for example, after a merger). You apply before the end of the relevant Tax Period, and you can do so while the merger is still being prepared. FTA Example 15 puts several rules together: C (the Parent), D and E form a group in 2024. C sells E on 1 May 2025, so E is out from 1 January 2025 . C and D carry on as a group. On 1 March 2026, C merges into D. Only one member is left, so the group ends that day . D, as C’s successor, files the group’s final return for 1 January to 28 February 2026 , due 30 November 2026 . D is also liable for any penalties on that return. D then files its own standalone return for the year to 31 December 2026. Two returns for one calendar year, from one surviving company. After a company leaves It keeps its own TRN . It doesn’t deregister, and it files standalone returns from then on. It stays jointly liable for the group’s tax for the years it was a member, unless that liability was limited. If it ceases to exist (dissolved or liquidated, rather than merged into another member), it must apply to deregister within 3 months . A company or group that has left can re What happens if a Tax Group member drops below 95% for a few days? It is treated as outside the group for the whole Tax Period. In FTA Example 12, seven days at 90% took the subsidiary out from 1 January, so it had to file its own return for the year. When does a sold subsidiary leave the Tax Group? From the start of the Tax Period in which the sale happens, along with any subsidiaries below it. The buyer can't group with it for that period either. Does a company deregister when it leaves a Tax Group? No. It keeps its own TRN and files standalone returns. It stays jointly liable for the group's tax for the years it was a member.

t: The 95% Test: Can Your Companies Form a UAE Tax Group?
d: The nine conditions to form a UAE Corporate Tax Group, and the 95% ownership traps in the FTA's examples: legal title, nominal value, chains, preferred shares.
c: Part 1 covered what a Tax Group gets you. This part covers who qualifies. Most groups that fail don’t fail on the obvious conditions. They fail on how “95%” is measured. The nine conditions Under Article 40(1) of the Corporate Tax Law, the Parent Company and every Subsidiary must be: Juridical persons. Companies qualify. A sole establishment run by an individual doesn’t. An ordinary unincorporated partnership doesn’t either, unless the FTA has approved it as a Taxable Person in its own right. UAE Resident Persons , and not treated as tax resident in another country under a tax treaty the UAE has in force. 95% share capital. The Parent owns at least 95%, directly or through Subsidiaries. 95% voting rights. 95% of profits and net assets. Both tests must be met. Not Exempt Persons. That rules out Government Entities themselves, though their taxable subsidiaries can group in certain cases. Not Qualifying Free Zone Persons. A free zone company that isn’t a QFZP can join, and so can a QFZP that has elected to pay the standard rates. On the same Financial Year. Using the same Accounting Standards. All IFRS, or all IFRS for SMEs, but not a mix. And the rule that catches people out: every condition must be met continuously for the whole Tax Period. Miss one for a single day and that company is out of the group from the start of the year (Part 3). Trap 1: indirect ownership only counts through Subsidiaries Indirect holdings count, but only through companies that are themselves in the group . Percentages multiply down the chain: Example 6: A owns 95% of B, and B owns 95% of C. A’s indirect stake in C is 95% × 95% = 90.25% , so C can’t join A’s group. B and C could form their own group, but B can only be in one group at a time. Example 7: D owns 50% of F directly and 95% of E, and E owns the other 50% of F. D’s total stake in F is 50% + (95% × 50%) = 97.5% , so F can join. It also means one non-qualifying company in the middle breaks the chain for everything below it. In Example 4 , the middle company P is a Qualifying Free Zone Person. So N can group with neither P nor P’s 100% subsidiary Q. Trap 2: a foreign parent can’t be in the group A foreign company that isn’t UAE resident can’t be a member. Its UAE subsidiaries can still group, but only under a UAE resident Parent Company . In Example 1, foreign Company F owns two separate UAE holding companies, E and D. You end up with two Tax Groups (E with A, B and C; D with G), not one. E and D are linked only through the foreign parent, so neither can be the Parent of the other. What to do about it: if you want one UAE group, you need one UAE holding company above all the UAE entities. Trap 3: how “95%” is measured Legal title, not economic ownership (Example 2). H owns 80% of J and buys the economic rights to the other 20%, but K keeps the legal title. The share capital test looks at legal ownership, so H fails at 80%. Nominee arrangements don’t count. Nominal value, not share count (Example 3). M holds 100 of L’s 101 shares, which is 99% by count. But M’s shares are worth AED 10 each and the one share M doesn’t hold is worth AED 1,000. By nominal value M owns 50%, and fails. Profit entitlement can drop below 95% (Example 9). A preferred shareholder takes a fixed AED 0.1m dividend. In a year with AED 3m profit, the ordinary shareholder gets 96.67% and passes. In a year with AED 0.15m profit, it gets 33.33%. The group then ends from the start of that year , and the FTA must be notified within 20 business days of the year end. Also: convertible loans, warrants and options don’t count as share capital. On voting rights, non-voting shares are excluded, but a minority holder’s right to appoint a director doesn’t break the test by itself as long as the Parent keeps at least 95% of shareholder votes. Fixing a Financial Year mismatch If everything else lines up but the year-ends don’t, a company can apply to the FTA to change its Tax Period. The adjusted period can’t be shorter than 6 months or long How is indirect ownership counted for the 95% test? Percentages multiply down the chain, and only through companies that are themselves in the group. If A owns 95% of B and B owns 95% of C, A's stake in C is 90.25%, so C can't join A's group. Can a foreign parent company be in a UAE Tax Group? No. A non-resident company can't be a member. Its UAE subsidiaries can only group under a UAE resident Parent Company. Does the 95% test use the number of shares? No. It uses legal ownership measured by nominal value. Holding 99% of shares by count can be only 50% by nominal value, which fails the test.

t: One Return for the Whole Group, and One Shared Tax Bill: UAE Corporate Tax Groups Explained
d: What a UAE Corporate Tax Group is, what it saves (one return, pooled losses, tax-free intra-group transfers) and the joint liability every member takes on.
c: If you run two or more UAE companies under common ownership, you’ve probably been asked whether you should form a Tax Group. It sounds like pure admin relief: one return instead of five. It’s more than that, in both directions. This is Part 1 of a 6-part series based on the FTA’s updated Corporate Tax Guide on Tax Groups (CTGTGR1, November 2026) . The series uses the FTA’s own worked examples throughout. What a Tax Group is A Tax Group is two or more UAE resident companies that the FTA treats as a single Taxable Person under Article 40 of the Corporate Tax Law. The Parent Company files one Tax Return for all of them, based on one set of Aggregated Financial Statements . Three things to know up front: It’s optional. A Tax Group only exists if the companies apply and the FTA approves. It isn’t a VAT group. A Corporate Tax Group is a separate regime from a VAT tax group. Having one doesn’t give you the other. The businesses don’t have to be related. A trading company and a property company can group, as long as the ownership and other conditions are met (Part 2). There’s no cap on the number of members. Each company can be in only one Tax Group at a time, though, and a Parent Company can’t split its subsidiaries into several groups. What you gain, and what you give up The gains: One Tax Return and one payment, handled by the Parent Company. Losses offset automatically. A loss in one member reduces another member’s profit in the same year, with no loss transfer paperwork. Intra-group transactions are eliminated. Management fees, intra-group sales and asset transfers between members drop out of the taxable result (subject to the 2-year clawback in Part 5). What you give up: One 0% band, not several. The 0% rate applies to the first AED 375,000 of the group’s Taxable Income, however many companies are in it. Five companies filing separately each get their own band. Small Business Relief is tested on the group. The AED 3 million revenue test applies to the group’s combined revenue. An extra audit. The Aggregated Financial Statements need a special purpose audit every year (Part 4). The decision usually comes down to whether the pooled losses and eliminated intra-group charges are worth more than the extra 0% bands you give up, plus the cost of the audit. What the Parent Company takes on The Parent Company represents the group. It applies to form the group and for every later change, prepares and audits the Aggregated Financial Statements, files the single return and pays the tax within 9 months of the year end, and keeps the records. That includes transfer pricing documentation. Registration works like this: Every company needs its own Corporate Tax TRN before applying. Once the FTA approves, the group gets a separate TRN . Members are not deregistered . They keep their own TRNs, which they’ll need again if they ever leave. The trade-off nobody mentions: joint liability This is the part that should change how you think about grouping: Every member is jointly and severally liable for the group’s Corporate Tax, for every Tax Period it was a member. That liability stays with the company after it leaves the group. Administrative penalties are different. They stay with the Parent Company, because joint and several liability doesn’t extend to penalties. You can apply to limit it. A Tax Group can ask the FTA to limit joint and several liability to one or more members. The FTA decides case by case. Why this matters in a deal: if you’re buying a company that has ever been in a Tax Group, the group’s unpaid tax for those years is a liability of the company you’re buying. Put it on the due diligence checklist. Should you form one? It’s usually worth a serious look when: one company makes losses (a start-up arm, a new branch) and another makes steady profits, there are significant intra-group charges or asset transfers, or the group is already preparing IFRS accounts for every entity anyway. It’s usually not worth it when: each company’s profit  Is a Corporate Tax Group the same as a VAT group? No. A Corporate Tax Group is a separate regime under Article 40 of the Corporate Tax Law. Having a VAT group doesn't give you a Corporate Tax Group, or the other way round. Does each company in a Tax Group get its own 0% band? No. The group gets one 0% band on the first AED 375,000 of its combined Taxable Income, however many members it has. Who is liable for a Tax Group's Corporate Tax? Every member is jointly and severally liable for the group's Corporate Tax for the periods it was a member, even after it leaves. Administrative penalties stay with the Parent Company, and the group can apply to the FTA to limit joint liability.
